articles.title: Anthropic's 100 Overcharge Bug: What Internationalization Failures Reveal About Agent Payment Pipelines
articles.excerpt: A Costa Rican developer tried to load $100 in API credits on Anthropic's console. The platform charged $10,000 instead. The root cause was a missing decimal separator validation layer that silently in…
articles.body: A Costa Rican developer tried to load $100 in API credits on Anthropic's console. The platform charged $10,000 instead. The root cause was a missing decimal separator validation layer that silently interpreted "100,00" (Spanish locale format) as 10000. No confirmation modal. No server-side normalization. Just an instant charge 100 times larger than intended. This is not a UX annoyance. It is a structural failure in the payment authorization boundary that sits between agent consumption metering and financial settlement. Every agent platform that bills for API calls faces this exact problem: how do you validate currency input across locales without trusting client-side formatting?

articles.body: Every week a new agent skills pack shows up on GitHub Trending. I installed a few. Then a few more. Then I copied skills from three different packs into one folder. That is when things got weird. Two skills had the same name. The agent picked one at random. Two more had almost identical descriptions, so both triggered on the same prompt. One skill had no description at all, so the agent never picked it. I had no idea until I started reading every SKILL.md by hand. So I built a tiny tool to do that reading for me: skill-audit .

articles.title: Go Profiling in Production: pprof, Flamegraphs and Memory Leaks
articles.excerpt: Your Go service handles thousands of requests per minute — until it doesn't. Memory climbs steadily, p99 latency spikes, and the first instinct is to add more instances. Before doing that, you need to…
articles.body: Your Go service handles thousands of requests per minute — until it doesn't. Memory climbs steadily, p99 latency spikes, and the first instinct is to add more instances. Before doing that, you need to understand what the code is actually doing. Go's built-in profiling tooling makes this tractable without third-party frameworks or expensive APM subscriptions. Setting Up pprof in a Running Service pprof is part of the standard library. Adding it to an existing HTTP service takes four lines: import ( "net/http" _ "net/http/pprof" ) func main () { // Expose pprof on a separate internal port — never public go func () { http . ListenAndServe ( "localhost:6060" , nil ) }() // ... rest of your server setup } The blank import registers the pprof HTTP handlers automatically.

articles.title: I built a handheld mmWave presence radar, and the first bug was a board that never ran my code
articles.excerpt: One small device noticing one thing. That's the demo genre I keep falling for, and this time it's an M5Stack Cardputer-Adv with an LD2410 mmWave sensor hanging off its EXT header. The firmware turns t…
articles.body: One small device noticing one thing. That's the demo genre I keep falling for, and this time it's an M5Stack Cardputer-Adv with an LD2410 mmWave sensor hanging off its EXT header. The firmware turns the sensor's UART stream into a radar scope on the handheld's 240 by 135 screen: a sweep line rotating through the cone the sensor watches, roughly 60 degrees, a contact sitting at a radius equal to the measured distance, a trail fading behind it as the target moves, and a NO PRESENCE state when the room is empty. No app, no phone in between. The device itself knows someone is approaching. Writing the firmware was the easy part. The hard part was getting a single byte back out of the board.

articles.excerpt: The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22, bringing a spectacular display of shooting stars to the autumn sky.
articles.body: The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22, triggering a spectacular display of shooting stars as Earth plunges through the densest part of the debris trail shed by Halley's Comet. Here's what you need to know. When is the best time to see Orionid shooting stars? Orionid meteors are best spotted between the hours of midnight and dawn on Oct. 22, when 10-20 shooting stars may be seen brightening the night sky each hour under ideal dark-sky. The glare cast by the 74%-lit waxing gibbous moon will hide fainter shooting stars for much of the night. Thankfully, the lunar disk will set a few hours after midnight, leaving a window of beautifully dark sky before dawn in which to enjoy the full majesty of the annual meteor shower.

Instead of Face ID, it uses Touch ID on the power button. It has two cameras, a main lens and a wide-angle lens. Apple completely revamped iOS 27’s controls and apps for the foldable, including putting the dock on the side of the phone. And it has a flashy opening animation when you unfold the phone. The iPhone Duo a big new bet from Apple, though one that’s a little late to the game compared to competitors like Samsung and Google. The phone isn’t cheap: it starts at $1,999 for the base 256GB model, and the prices only go up from there.

But it also highlights how fragile that life is, tethered to our lonely Earth in the vast void of space, according to Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir of NASA. "You see this very thin, tenuous band of an atmosphere , and you know that that is all that is supporting life, and we really need to do our best to protect it," Meir said on Thursday afternoon (Oct. 15), during a press conference that discussed the recently concluded Crew-12 mission .

articles.body: I used to think being interested in the night sky meant I had to try every meteor shower. If a calendar said "peak," I interpreted that as an instruction. I'd set an alarm, find several layers of clothing and go outside at around 2:00 a.m. when even the neighborhood cats seemed surprised to see me. Then I'd spend an increasingly resentful 45 minutes staring upward, occasionally see one meteor and wonder whether I was somehow doing it all wrong. As I've grown into stargazing, I've become much more selective. The Orionids peak next week, and normally I'd be tempted. These fast meteors come from debris from Halley's Comet , which is enough of a connection to make almost anyone want to go outside.

articles.title: Scientists find 'gemstones' in atmosphere of bizarre, scorching-hot 'marshmallow' exoplanet
articles.excerpt: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have unravelled some of the secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot exoplanet that has the consistency of marshmallow.
articles.body: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have unraveled some of the atmospheric secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot world that has the consistency of marshmallow. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , under the watchful infrared eye of the JWST , is WASP-17b, located around 1,300 light-years away. The exoplanet has a mass around 0.8 times that of Jupiter, but it is around twice as wide as the solar system's largest planet, giving it a "super-puff" consistency comparable to the Earth-based treat. WASP-17 b is so close to its parent star that it completes an orbit in under four Earth days, with this proximity also making the temperature of this " hot Jupiter " skyrocket.

articles.title: How to see the Orionid meteor shower 2026 peak this week — and when to look
articles.excerpt: The Orionids peak around Oct. 21. Here's when and where to look for the best chance of spotting meteors.
articles.body: If you love watching meteors, 2026 has given you plenty to enjoy. This summer, the annual Perseid meteor shower peaked on the day of a new moon — and a solar eclipse — so moonlight stayed out of the way. And there's more to look forward to: in December, the Geminids, the year's most prolific shower, will peak after a waxing crescent moon sets early in the evening, opening the door to excellent viewing. Right between those two headline showers, the dependable Orionids take their turn, reaching peak activity around Oct. 21-22. So, when and where can you catch the show?
